questions.question: Let $A\colon V\to W$ be linear, where $V$ has ordered basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $n=3$ vectors and $W$ has ordered basis $\mathcal{C}$ of $m=5$ vectors. What is the size of the matrix representation $[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}$?
options: $3\times5$: one row per vector of $\mathcal{B}$, one column per vector of $\mathcal{C}$
$5\times3$: one row per vector of $\mathcal{C}$, one column per vector of $\mathcal{B}$
$5\times5$: square of the size of the codomain basis $\mathcal{C}$
$3\times3$: square of the size of the domain basis $\mathcal{B}$

questions.question: Let $A\colon V\to W$ be linear with ordered bases $\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_n)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal{C}=(\boldsymbol{w}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{w}_m)$ of $W$. What is the entry $a_{ij}$ of $[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}$?
options: The coefficient of $\boldsymbol{w}_i$ when $A\boldsymbol{v}_j$ is written in the basis $\mathcal{C}$
The coefficient of $\boldsymbol{w}_j$ when $A\boldsymbol{v}_i$ is written in the basis $\mathcal{C}$
The coefficient of $\boldsymbol{v}_i$ when $A\boldsymbol{v}_j$ is written in the basis $\mathcal{B}$
The $i$-th standard coordinate of the image vector $A\boldsymbol{v}_j$ in $W$

questions.question: Let $A\colon V\to W$ be linear with ordered bases $\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_3)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $W$. Let $\mathcal{B}'=(\boldsymbol{v}_2,\boldsymbol{v}_1,\boldsymbol{v}_3)$ list the same vectors with the first two swapped. How is $[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}'}$ obtained from $[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}$?
options: By swapping its first and second columns
By swapping its first and second rows
It is the same matrix, since the basis vectors are the same
By transposing it, since the order of the input changes

questions.question: Let $A\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$ be linear, with ordered bases $\mathcal{B}$ (domain) and $\mathcal{C}$ (codomain) that differ from each other and from the standard basis. Which product gives the coordinate vector $[A\boldsymbol{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}$ for every $\boldsymbol{v}\in\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: $[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}\,[\boldsymbol{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}$, using the $\mathcal{C}$-coordinates of $\boldsymbol{v}$
$[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}\,[\boldsymbol{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}$, using the $\mathcal{B}$-coordinates of $\boldsymbol{v}$
$[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}\,\boldsymbol{v}$, using the standard coordinates of $\boldsymbol{v}$
$[\boldsymbol{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}^{\top}\,[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}$, a row vector times the matrix

questions.question: For a linear $A\colon V\to W$, the entries of $[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}$ are read off from $A\boldsymbol{v}_j=\sum_{i=1}^m a_{ij}\boldsymbol{w}_i$, where $\mathcal{C}=(\boldsymbol{w}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{w}_m)$. Which property of $\mathcal{C}$ guarantees that the numbers $a_{ij}$ are uniquely determined?
options: The vectors $\boldsymbol{w}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{w}_m$ are linearly independent.
The vectors $\boldsymbol{w}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{w}_m$ span the space $W$.
The map $A$ is linear, so it respects combinations.
The basis $\mathcal{C}$ has as many vectors as the basis $\mathcal{B}$.

questions.question: Let $A\colon\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2$ be the linear map $A(x,y,z)=(x+2z,\;y-z)$. What is its matrix representation with respect to the standard bases?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}1&0&2\\0&1&-1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}1&0&2\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: Let $M\colon P_1\to P_2$, $p(t)\mapsto t\,p(t)$, where $P_k$ is the space of real polynomials of degree at most $k$, with ordered bases $(1,t)$ of $P_1$ and $(1,t,t^2)$ of $P_2$. What is the matrix representation of $M$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: Let $A\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$, $A(x,y)=(x+y,\,x-y)$, with the standard basis $\mathcal{E}$ in the domain and $\mathcal{C}=\big((1,1)^{\top},(1,-1)^{\top}\big)$ in the codomain. What is $[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{E}}$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{1}{2}&\tfrac{1}{2}\\ \tfrac{1}{2}&-\tfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: Let $P_2$ be the space of real polynomials of degree at most $2$ and $\mathcal{L}(P_2,\mathbb{R}^4)$ the vector space of linear maps $P_2\to\mathbb{R}^4$. Using matrix representations with respect to fixed bases, what is $\dim\mathcal{L}(P_2,\mathbb{R}^4)$?

Let $A\colon V\to V$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional space and $\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{v}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{v}_n)$ an ordered basis such that the second column of $[A]_{\mathcal{B}}$ is zero. What follows about $A$?
options: $A$ may be invertible, since another basis can give an invertible matrix.
$A$ is not invertible, as it sends the basis vector $\boldsymbol{v}_2$ to $\boldsymbol{0}$.
$A$ is the zero map, since a zero column forces all images to vanish.
The second row of $[A]_{\mathcal{B}}$ must be zero as well, as $A$ is an operator.

questions.question: A linear map $A\colon V\to W$ has representation $[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}$ for ordered bases $\mathcal{B}$ of $V$ and $\mathcal{C}=(\boldsymbol{w}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{w}_m)$ of $W$. Let $\mathcal{C}'=(2\boldsymbol{w}_1,\boldsymbol{w}_2,\ldots,\boldsymbol{w}_m)$. How does $[A]_{\mathcal{C}',\mathcal{B}}$ differ from $[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}$?
options: Its first row is halved; all other entries are unchanged.
Its first row is doubled; all other entries are unchanged.
Its first column is halved; all other entries are unchanged.
It is unchanged, since the map $A$ itself is the same.

questions.question: On real polynomial spaces $P_k$ (degree at most $k$), let $M\colon P_1\to P_2$, $p\mapsto tp$, with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, and $D\colon P_2\to P_1$, $p\mapsto p'$, with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}$, in the bases $(1,t)$ and $(1,t,t^2)$. What is the matrix of $DM\colon P_1\to P_1$ in the basis $(1,t)$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$
Undefined, as $2\times3$ times $3\times2$ is not defined
$\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: Let $S\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$, $S(x,y)=(y,x)$, and let $\mathcal{B}=\big((1,0)^{\top},(1,1)^{\top}\big)$ be used in both domain and codomain. What is $[S]_{\mathcal{B}}$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: Let $P_1$ be the real polynomials of degree at most $1$ with ordered basis $\mathcal{B}=(1+t,\;t)$, and $A\colon P_1\to\mathbb{R}^2$ linear with $[A]_{\mathcal{E},\mathcal{B}}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&6\end{pmatrix}$ for the standard basis $\mathcal{E}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Which nonzero polynomial $p$ satisfies $A p=\boldsymbol{0}$?

Two linear maps $S,T\colon V\to W$ satisfy $[S]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}=[T]_{\mathcal{C}',\mathcal{B}'}$ for some ordered bases $\mathcal{B},\mathcal{B}'$ of $V$ and $\mathcal{C},\mathcal{C}'$ of $W$. Must $S=T$?
options: Yes, because $A\mapsto[A]$ is a bijection from linear maps to matrices.
Yes, provided the common matrix is square and invertible.
No: on $\mathbb{R}$, $x\mapsto x$ in bases $(1),(1)$ and $x\mapsto2x$ in $(1),(2)$ both give $(1)$.
Yes, as long as the domain bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{B}'$ coincide.

questions.question: Let $S(x)=(x,0)$ map $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2$ and $T(x,y)=x+2y$ map $\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$; $\mathbb{R}$ has basis $(1)$. In the standard basis $\mathcal{E}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$, $[S]=(1,0)^{\top}$; in $\mathcal{B}'=(\boldsymbol{e}_2,\boldsymbol{e}_1)$, $[T]=(2\;\,1)$. Is $(2\;\,1)(1,0)^{\top}=(2)$ the matrix of $TS$?
options: Yes; the product of two representing matrices always represents the composition.
No; the factors must be multiplied in reverse order, as $(1,0)^{\top}(2\;\,1)$.
No; the middle bases differ, and in fact $[TS]=(1)$.
Yes; $\mathcal{E}$ and $\mathcal{B}'$ contain the same vectors, so the bases agree.

questions.question: Let $P_2$ be the real polynomials of degree at most $2$, with ordered basis $\mathcal{B}$, and let $\mathcal{C}$ be an ordered basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$. For an arbitrary real $2\times3$ matrix $M$, how many linear maps $A\colon P_2\to\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfy $[A]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}=M$?
options: Exactly one, but only when $M$ has rank $2$
Infinitely many, since only basis images are fixed
Exactly one, but only when $\mathcal{B},\mathcal{C}$ are standard
Exactly one, for every such matrix $M$

questions.question: Let $R\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$, $R(x,y)=(-y,x)$, the quarter turn. With $\mathcal{B}=(\boldsymbol{e}_1,\boldsymbol{e}_2)$ and $\mathcal{C}=(\boldsymbol{e}_2,-\boldsymbol{e}_1)$ one finds $[R]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}=I_2$. Does this show that $1$ is an eigenvalue of $R$?
options: Yes: the diagonal entries of a representing matrix are eigenvalues of the map.
No: eigenvalues are read from $[R]_{\mathcal{B}}$, with one basis for input and output; here $\mathcal{C}\neq\mathcal{B}$.
Yes: $[R]_{\mathcal{C},\mathcal{B}}=I_2$ means that $R$ is the identity map, which has eigenvalue $1$.
Yes: each $R\boldsymbol{e}_j$ is a basis vector, so $\boldsymbol{e}_1,\boldsymbol{e}_2$ are eigenvectors with eigenvalue $1$.

questions.question: Let $V$ be the space of real $2\times2$ matrices with ordered basis $(E_{11},E_{12},E_{21},E_{22})$, where $E_{ij}$ has a $1$ in position $(i,j)$ and zeros elsewhere. What is the matrix representation of the linear operator $T(X)=X^{\top}$ in this basis?
options: The $4\times4$ identity matrix, since $T$ maps each $E_{ij}$ to a basis matrix
The $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, since $T$ swaps the off-diagonal entries
The $4\times4$ matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,1)$, since $T$ flips the off-diagonal part
The $4\times4$ matrix that swaps the second and third coordinates and fixes the others
